e.etymology: A spelling of Evelyn used in Hungarian, Estonian and Spanish. Evelyn comes from the Norman French name Aveline, built on a Germanic root avi of uncertain meaning, perhaps desired.
Often a spelling of Nia, which is Swahili for purpose and one of the seven principles of Kwanzaa. Nia is also a Welsh form of the Irish name Niamh, bright.

assoc.t: Nya, the water ninja in Lego Ninjago

e.etymology: From Hebrew Adah, ornament. In Genesis she is a wife of Lamech, the first woman named in the Bible after Eve, and another Adah is a wife of Esau. It is separate from the Germanic name Ada.
Hawaiian ka inoa, the name or the namesake, first given as a second name to a child named after a relative. It was later also read as kai noa, sea free of taboo.
A modern name, a spelling of Aliana, which extends Alana or Eliana with the -iana ending of Ariana and Liliana.
A spelling of Finn, from Irish Fionn, fair or white, the name of the legendary hero Fionn mac Cumhaill. The y spelling is especially popular in Germany.
A spelling of Anya, the Russian pet form of Anna, which goes back to Hebrew Channah (grace, favor).

e.meaning: French form of Mary, also read as Marie plus Anne
e.etymology: The French form of Mariamne, an old variant of Mary, from Hebrew Miriam. In 18th-century France it was also understood as Marie joined to Anne, and it became the name of the figure who personifies the French Republic.
namesakes: Marianne Williamson (self-help author and presidential candidate)
Marianne Dashwood (the romantic sister in Sense and Sensibility)

assoc.t: Marianne, the female symbol of the French Republic
Marianne Dashwood of Sense and Sensibility

e.etymology: A spelling of Danica, a Slavic name from the word for the morning star, the planet Venus seen at dawn.

assoc.t: Danica Patrick, race car driver (spelled Danica)

e.etymology: A Yiddish pet form of Menachem, Hebrew for comforter. Mendel is also a south German surname, the one borne by the monk Gregor Mendel.

assoc.t: Gregor Mendel, the monk who founded genetics

e.etymology: A spelling of Maisie, the Scottish pet form of Mairead (Margaret), from Greek margarites, pearl.

assoc.t: Maisy the mouse of the children's picture books (as Maisy)

e.etymology: A modern coinage, probably Gabrielle with the first letter dropped, in the same family as Brielle and Aubrielle. Gabrielle is the French feminine of Gabriel.
A modern American coinage that joins a La- or Lani opening to the -iyah ending of names such as Aniyah and Saniyah.
A spelling of Bryson, an English surname meaning son of Brice. Brice is an old saint's name of Gaulish origin.
A modern spelling with no single source: families use it for Riya, Rhea or Raya, or as a short form of names ending in -riah such as Mariah.
e.note: Expect to say whether it is RYE-uh or REE-uh.

e.etymology: In English a variant of Leila, from Arabic layla, night, which reached English through 19th-century literature. Lela is also a separate Georgian name. It was most popular in the US around 1900.
A French pet form of Josephine, the feminine of Joseph, from Hebrew Yosef, he will add.
The Russian form of Helen, from Greek Helene by way of Latin Helena. The Greek name is of uncertain origin and is often linked to a word for torch or bright light.

assoc.t: Yelena Belova, Marvel's Black Widow (Florence Pugh)

e.etymology: The medieval English form of Maurice, from Latin Mauritius, a Moor. It became a surname and was later taken up again as a first name, most often in the early 1900s.
namesakes: Morris Chestnut (actor in Boyz n the Hood and The Best Man)
Morris Day (singer of The Time in Purple Rain)

assoc.t: Morris the Cat, 9Lives cat food mascot
morris dancing, the English folk dance

e.etymology: A modern spelling of Connor, the English form of Irish Conchobhar, lover of hounds or wolves, the name of a legendary king of Ulster.
A spelling of Clayton, an English place name and surname from Old English claeg (clay) and tun (settlement).

A name that spread in India in the 2000s and is now common in South Asian American families. It is usually treated as a form of Arabic Samira, an evening companion in conversation; its exact source is unclear.
A 20th-century variant of Diana, the Roman goddess whose name comes from a root for divine. It spread after 1936 through film star Deanna Durbin and is also used as a feminine of Dean.
namesakes: Deanna Durbin (singing film star of the 1930s and 1940s)
Deanna Troi (ship's counselor in Star Trek: The Next Generation)

e.etymology: From Arabic abd (servant) and al (the). It is the first half of compound names such as Abdullah, servant of God, and Abdul Rahman, servant of the Merciful, and is often used alone in English.

assoc.t: Paula Abdul, pop singer and American Idol judge

e.etymology: A spelling of Sheila that is popular in Latin America. Sheila is the English form of Irish Sile, the Irish version of Cecilia.
A spelling of Naomi used mainly in Spanish-speaking families. Naomi is Hebrew for pleasantness and is the name of Ruth's mother-in-law in the Bible. A Japanese name is also written Nahomi.
A form of Yasmin, the Persian and Arabic name of the jasmine flower and the source of English Jasmine.
A recent American coinage built from Kash, a spelling of Cash, and the -ton ending of names such as Easton and Paxton, here spelled -tyn.
A K spelling of Cove, the English word for a small sheltered bay, used as a given name only in the last few years.
From Sanskrit nila, dark blue, the color of sapphire and of the god Krishna's skin in Hindu tradition.
A spelling of Kason, a modern American name in the sound family of Mason, Jason and Grayson. Cason also exists as an English surname.

e.meaning: a cure, something that sets things right
e.etymology: The English word remedy, from Latin remedium, a cure. It joined the newer word names for girls in the 2020s.

assoc.t: Remedy Entertainment, video game studio behind Alan Wake
